36.title: Vishnu is born as Rama
36.hook: Dasharatha's long wait; God comes down as his son
36.carry: avatar: god comes down to set things right
36.howItsDone: Many Hindus read the Ramayana in their own language, recite it at home or in temples, and watch it performed as Ramlila each autumn; Rama's birthday is celebrated as Rama Navami in spring.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sankat mochan, and a mountain carried through the night. You've met Hanuman. Now, for five weeks, the whole story he lives inside.

Ayodhya. A shining city on a river, with walls and gardens and elephants, and a good king named Dasharatha. His name means ten chariots. He has wealth, peace, and three queens: Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. And no son. Year after year, the kingdom waits for an heir, and the king grows old. And far above Ayodhya, the gods have a problem of their own.

This is the opening of the Ramayana, the story of Rama. Tradition says Valmiki composed it, and calls him the first poet. For the next five weeks, i'll walk you through it, one scene a day. Here's the trouble above the clouds. A demon king, Ravana, has won a boon: no god, no demon, no spirit can kill him. He never thought to ask about humans; they seemed too small to matter. So the gods go to Vishnu, the preserver, and Vishnu makes a choice: he will be born as a human, as Dasharatha's son. Back on earth, Dasharatha holds a great fire ritual for sons, led by a young sage, Rishyashringa. Out of the flames rises a shining figure carrying a golden bowl of sweet rice pudding, payasa. Give this to your queens, he says. In time, four sons are born. Kausalya bears Rama. Kaikeyi bears Bharata. Sumitra bears twins, Lakshmana and Shatrughna. Remember the name Kaikeyi. Now, the big idea. Hindus call it avatara, a word that means coming down. Many Hindus believe that when the world tips badly out of balance, God doesn't only fix it from far away. God comes down, and is born as one of us: a baby, in a family, in a house with worried parents. Rama is honored as Vishnu's avatar. That's why, on Rama's birthday, Rama Navami, many temples and homes place a small image of baby Rama in a cradle and rock it at midday, the hour tradition gives for his birth. The old king asked for an heir. God came to live in his house.

37.title: Rama follows a guru
37.hook: the sage Vishvamitra; the bow no one can lift
37.howItsDone: Rama's youth, his journey with Vishvamitra and the lifting of Shiva's bow are favorite scenes in Ramlila plays and in children's retellings of the Ramayana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: putrakameshti, the fire ritual, and Vishnu born as Rama. Avatar: God comes down. Today, the boy who is God has to learn, and leave home to do it.

Four brothers grow up in a palace. Rama and Lakshmana are inseparable; so are Bharata and Shatrughna. Then a famous sage walks into the court: Vishvamitra. Demons keep ruining his sacrifices in the forest, and he wants help. Not the army. Not the king. He wants Rama, who is, the text says, not yet sixteen. Dasharatha, who waited so long for this boy, panics. Take my army, take me, he says, just not my son. The family priest, Vasishtha, gently tells him: let him go. He'll be safe with this teacher, and he'll need what he learns.
screen: `FOUR BROTHERS.` → `THE SAGE WANTS RAMA.` → `NOT YET SIXTEEN.` → `LET HIM GO.`

segments.voice: So Rama and Lakshmana follow the sage into the forest. In the tradition, Rama is Vishnu born human, and still he has to learn. On a riverbank the sage teaches the boys two mantras, bala and atibala, so they won't feel hunger or tiredness, and later he gives Rama divine weapons. Rama guards the sage's sacrifice and drives the demons off. One demon, Maricha, is hurled far out into the sea by a single arrow, and survives. Hold on to his name; he'll be back. This is the bond Hindus call guru and shishya, teacher and student. Guru is often explained as the one who removes darkness, and a guru gives more than facts: a mantra, a way of living, courage. That's why many Hindus touch a teacher's feet, why there's a day each year to honor teachers, Guru Purnima, and why in many families a child's first letters begin with a prayer and a teacher's hand guiding theirs. If God, born as a prince, still walked behind a teacher, nobody is too grand to learn. Then the sage takes them to Mithila. In King Janaka's court sits a bow that once belonged to Shiva himself, so heavy, in Valmiki's telling, that it's wheeled in on an iron cart dragged by thousands of men. Not one king could even lift it. Whoever strings it may marry Janaka's daughter, Sita. Rama walks up and lifts it as if it were nothing. Tomorrow: what happens when he tries to string it.

segments.voice: In many Hindu homes you greet a teacher by bowing, palms together, or by touching their feet. Picture one teacher who changed you: a grandparent, a coach, a guru. Put your palms together, bow your head a little, and thank them by name. If you don't pray, just say their name and what they gave you.

38.title: Sita's swayamvara
38.howItsDone: The wedding of Rama and Sita is celebrated as Vivah Panchami in parts of India and Nepal, especially around Janakpur; the breaking of the bow is a high point of Ramlila, and Hindu weddings keep a garland exchange, the jaimala.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vishvamitra led Rama out, and Rama lifted the bow no one else could. Even Rama needed a guru. Today, he tries to string it.

Years ago, King Janaka was plowing a field for a ritual, and his plow turned up something in the furrow: a baby girl, lying in the earth. He took her home, raised her as his daughter, and named her Sita, which means furrow. A daughter of the earth itself. Now she's grown, and her father has set the test: the man who strings Shiva's bow may marry her. Rama holds the great bow. He bends it and pulls the string toward its notch. And the bow, which no one else could even move, snaps in half with a crack like thunder. The text says people in the hall fell to the ground from the sound.
screen: `A BABY IN A FURROW.` → `SITA MEANS FURROW.` → `THE BOW SNAPS.` → `A CRACK LIKE THUNDER.`

segments.voice: Today's title uses the word swayamvara. Swayam means self; vara means choice, or the chosen groom. Swayamvara: choosing for yourself, an old custom in the epics where a princess chooses her husband, often with a garland. Here the versions part. In Valmiki's Ramayana, strictly speaking, this isn't a choosing. Janaka had promised Sita as the prize of strength: whoever strings the bow wins her. But in the Ramcharitmanas, the Hindi retelling by the poet Tulsidas, there's a scene before the contest. Sita walks into a flower garden to pray and sees Rama there, picking flowers for his teacher. She falls in love on the spot and prays to the goddess Parvati that he'll be the one. When the bow breaks, she walks forward and puts the victory garland around his neck. She chooses. Both tellings are held dear. And in devotion, Sita is no prize at all: tradition says she is the goddess Lakshmi herself. Here's where it shows up in a Hindu home. Devotees rarely say Rama alone. They say Sita-Ram, or Siya-Ram, with her name first. At Ramlila and in temples the crowd shouts Siyavar Ramachandra ki jai: victory to Ramachandra, Sita's groom. Vara again, the same word as in swayamvara. Hindus often worship God as a couple, Sita-Ram, Radha-Krishna, Lakshmi-Narayan, and the goddess's name usually comes first. And when a Hindu bride and groom exchange garlands at a wedding today, the jaimala, many families think of this scene.

39.title: Kaikeyi's two wishes
39.hook: the maid Manthara; the old promise called in
39.howItsDone: Hindus retell Kaikeyi's wishes as the turning point of the Ramayana; in Ramlila performances it's often the moment the audience goes quiet, and many discuss how much blame Kaikeyi and Manthara bear.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita's swayamvara, a bow snapped and a garland placed. Sita-Ram, her name comes first. Today, years later in Ayodhya, a happy announcement goes wrong overnight.

Dasharatha is old now, and he makes the announcement the whole kingdom wants: tomorrow, Rama will be crowned as heir. The city goes wild. Flags, flowers, lamps in every window. In the palace, Queen Kaikeyi, Bharata's mother, hears the news and is delighted. She loves Rama. She even gives a jewel to the servant who brought the news: her old maid, Manthara, who came with her from her childhood home. Manthara throws the jewel down. Are you a fool? she says. When Rama is king, his mother will be queen mother, and you'll be her servant. And your son, Bharata, will have nothing.
screen: `TOMORROW, RAMA WILL BE CROWNED.` → `KAIKEYI IS DELIGHTED.` → `MANTHARA THROWS THE JEWEL DOWN.`

segments.voice: At first Kaikeyi argues: Rama is good, Rama is fair. But Manthara keeps talking, all night, and slowly the fear gets in. Then Manthara reminds her of something. Long ago, in a battle, Dasharatha was wounded, and Kaikeyi saved his life. In gratitude he promised her two wishes, anything she asked, and she never used them. Use them now. So Kaikeyi goes to the room where a queen goes when she is angry, throws off her jewelry, and lies on the bare floor. Dasharatha finds her there, frantic. I'll give you anything. She makes him swear it, on Rama's name. Then she asks. First wish: crown Bharata instead. Second wish: send Rama into the forest, in exile, for fourteen years. He begs and pleads all night. But he gave his word, and he can't take it back. Why not? Because Hinduism counts truth, satya, as part of dharma, and a promise is a truth about the future. Tulsidas's retelling puts it in a line Hindu families still quote: in Rama's family, the custom has always been, let life go, but never the given word. Pran jaye par vachan na jaye. Who is to blame? The tradition argues. In Valmiki, Kaikeyi and Manthara make a real, human choice. In some later tellings, the gods send the goddess Saraswati to turn Manthara's mind. People still debate whether a promise pulled out like this should bind. But the story is clear about the teaching: a word given in gratitude, years ago, is still a word.

40.title: Fourteen years
40.hook: Rama exiled; he accepts in one sentence
40.howItsDone: Many Hindus hold up Rama's acceptance of exile as the model of keeping one's word and duty; the scene is often retold when families talk about hard decisions and honoring parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Kaikeyi's two vara, old boons called in: Bharata crowned, Rama exiled. A given word is dharma. Now someone has to tell Rama, on the morning of his coronation.

Rama wakes up on his coronation morning. The city is decorated for him. The priests are ready. The water for the ceremony has been gathered from sacred rivers. A messenger comes: your father wants to see you. Rama walks into Kaikeyi's rooms expecting a blessing, and finds his father on the floor, unable to look at him, unable to speak. Kaikeyi speaks instead. Calmly, she tells him everything. Bharata will be king. You will go to the forest, dressed as a hermit, for fourteen years. Your father promised. Everyone in the room waits to see what Rama will do.
screen: `THE CORONATION MORNING.` → `HIS FATHER CAN'T SPEAK.` → `FOURTEEN YEARS IN THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Rama says, in effect: so be it. I'll go. He doesn't argue or bargain. He tells Kaikeyi he would have given the kingdom to Bharata gladly if anyone had simply asked. His only sorrow is that his father is in pain. Then he walks out. Valmiki notices one detail, and people have repeated it ever since: Rama's face didn't change. It looked the same when he heard he'd be king, and when he heard he'd be exiled. That isn't coldness. The people around him are anything but calm. His mother Kausalya is devastated. His brother Lakshmana is furious and ready to fight their father for the throne. Rama is the steady one, and he talks Lakshmana down. Why does he accept? Dharma, your third word: doing what's yours to do. For Rama, keeping his father's word is his duty, even when it costs him everything. That's why tradition calls him maryada purushottam: the ideal person, who keeps within the bounds of right action. Not everyone finds this easy. Some readers ask whether Rama should have fought, and the tradition lets them ask. But the scene draws a line worth keeping: giving up and accepting are different. Giving up sits down. Accepting stands up and starts walking. Rama doesn't pretend it's fair; he just refuses to let the unfairness decide who he is. Hinduism has a whole teaching for this: do what's yours to do, and let go of how it turns out. Dharma: accept, then walk.
screen: `SO BE IT. I'LL GO.` · `HIS FACE DIDN'T CHANGE.` · `DHARMA: KEEP THE FATHER'S WORD.` · `ACCEPTING ISN'T GIVING UP.` · then, large: `DHARMA: ACCEPT, THEN WALK.`

segments.voice: Think of something in your life that isn't fair and won't change: a diagnosis, a loss, a decision someone else made. Don't argue with it for now; let your face be still, the way Rama's was. Breathe in: this is what is. Breathe out: what's mine to do next? If you pray, offer the next step to God, the way Rama gave his to dharma.
Fourteen years. Rama's exile, accepted in a sentence, on the morning he was meant to be crowned.
Your line: dharma, accept, then walk. Even fourteen years begin with one step. That's forty days in.

41.title: Sita insists
41.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Sita as a model of loyalty and strength; her insistence on going into exile is retold at weddings, in Ramlila, and in women's songs across India.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fourteen years, an exile accepted in a sentence. Dharma, dharma: accept, then walk. Now Rama goes to tell his wife, and he expects her to stay.

Rama finds Sita in their rooms, still dressed for the coronation. He tells her. Then he tells her what he's decided for her: stay here in the palace, where you're safe. Honor my father. Be kind to Bharata. Wait for me. He describes the forest, to make sure she understands. Thorns on the paths. Lions and snakes. Cold nights on the bare ground. Hunger, heat, wind. No place for a princess. He thinks he's protecting her. He thinks the conversation is over. It isn't.
screen: `STAY HERE, WHERE IT'S SAFE.` → `THORNS, LIONS, COLD, HUNGER.` → `HE THINKS IT'S OVER.`

segments.voice: In Valmiki's Ramayana, Sita doesn't answer quietly. A wife shares her husband's fortune, whatever it is, she tells him. If you're going into the forest today, I'll go ahead of you and walk down the thorns and the sharp grass, so your path is softer. With you, the forest is a palace. He keeps refusing, so she gets sharper. She asks, in effect, whether her father married her to someone with a man's shape but not a man's courage, if he'll leave his wife behind out of fear. She weeps. And Rama gives in. She comes. Notice who wins this argument. Sita isn't following orders; she's overruling them. The prince who calmly accepted exile from his father can't win an argument with his wife. The tradition calls a wife sahadharmini: the one who shares dharma. Sita takes that literally. His path of dharma is her path too, and she won't let him walk it alone. You can still see this at a Hindu wedding. The couple circle the sacred fire together and take seven steps, the saptapadi, and the old words say, roughly: with these seven steps, be my friend. Partners, not owner and follower. People read Sita's scene in more than one way. Some see the model of devotion in marriage. Others hear, especially in that sharp line, a woman with her own will, choosing her own life. Both readings live in the tradition. Neighbors have a line like it: in the Hebrew Bible, Ruth tells her mother-in-law that where she goes, Ruth will go.
screen: `I'LL WALK AHEAD, ON THE THORNS.` · `SHE OVERRULES HIM.` · `SAHADHARMINI: SHARING DHARMA.` · `SEVEN STEPS: BE MY FRIEND.` · then, large: `PARTNERS IN DHARMA.`

segments.voice: Picture someone whose path you share: a partner, a sibling, a friend, a child. Walk seven slow steps, in your room or in your head, and with each one, name one thing you'd carry for them. Then ask the harder question: who would walk into a forest for you? If you pray, give thanks for them; if you don't, just let their face come.

42.title: Lakshmana follows
42.carry: seva: serving is a way to love god
42.howItsDone: In many Hindu temples and home shrines, Rama is shown with Sita on one side and Lakshmana on the other, often with Hanuman kneeling before them; Lakshmana is honored as the model of a devoted brother.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita insists, and argues her way into the forest. Sahadharmini, partners in dharma. Two are going now. Today, a third, and the end of the week.

Nobody asked Lakshmana to go. Nobody exiled him. He could stay in the palace for fourteen years, a prince, with his own wife, Urmila, and a comfortable life. Rama even tells him to stay: look after our mothers, look after the kingdom. Lakshmana falls at his brother's feet and says no. The two have been inseparable since they were boys; the text says Rama couldn't sleep unless Lakshmana was beside him, couldn't eat unless he ate too. So Lakshmana says: I'll go ahead of you with a bow. I'll dig for roots and gather fruit. I'll keep watch while you and Sita sleep. Just don't leave me here.
screen: `NOBODY EXILED HIM.` → `STAY, RAMA SAYS.` → `I'LL KEEP WATCH WHILE YOU SLEEP.`

segments.voice: Then Lakshmana goes to say goodbye to his own mother, Sumitra, and she blesses him. In Valmiki's words, roughly: think of Rama as your father, Dasharatha. Think of Sita as me, your mother. Think of the forest as Ayodhya, your home. Now go, my son. Home is wherever these people are. Hindus have a word for what Lakshmana does: seva, service. Not service for pay, but service as love, and here, service to God, since Rama is Vishnu born human. Lakshmana carries the bags, builds the hut, stays awake. That's why, in the Ram darbar, the picture of Rama's court in many Hindu homes and temples, Lakshmana stands right beside Rama and Sita, and Hanuman kneels at their feet: two great servants, honored next to God. In temples today, people still do seva: sweeping, cooking, serving food, handing out prasad. The story is honest about the cost, too. Lakshmana leaves his wife, Urmila, behind for fourteen years, and Valmiki says almost nothing about her. Later tellings filled the silence: in one well-known folk version, she sleeps for fourteen years so her husband can stay awake. Now look back at this week. God came down as a baby. Even Rama walked behind a guru. A garland put Sita's name first. A king kept a word that broke him. A prince accepted his dharma in one breath. A wife claimed her share of it. And a brother nobody asked, went anyway, to serve.
screen: `THINK OF THE FOREST AS AYODHYA.` · `SEVA: SERVICE AS LOVE.` · `URMILA, LEFT BEHIND.` · `A WEEK OF THE RAMAYANA.` · then, large: `SEVA.`

segments.voice: Plan one small seva for today, without being asked and without telling anyone: wash someone's dishes, carry someone's bags, help at your temple. If you pray, offer it to God, the way Lakshmana served Rama; if you don't, offer it to the person. And spare a thought for the Urmilas, the people who stay behind so someone else can go.
